lines: You opened an app today without deciding to. Your thumb did it for you.
Then it kept moving. One more post. One more video. One more bad headline. And somewhere in there, an hour disappeared.
This is a film about the thing in your pocket that has no bottom. And about how to get your time back.
It has a name. Doomscrolling. Endlessly scrolling through bad news, long after it has stopped helping you.
And it has a cousin. In December twenty twenty four, Oxford University Press named brain rot its word of the year, and said use of the term had risen two hundred and thirty percent in a year.
So this is not just you. It is a pattern. And patterns have causes.
Cause number one. Nothing tells you to stop. A book has chapters. A show has an ending. A feed has neither.

The designer who built infinite scroll, Aza Raskin, has said he regrets it. In one talk, he estimated it wastes on the order of a hundred thousand human lifetimes every day. That is his estimate, and numbers like this are hard to check. But the point stands. The design removed the stopping point.
When there is no natural end, the only way to stop is to decide to stop. And deciding is the part that is hardest to do when you are tired.
Cause number two. You never know what is coming next. Maybe the next post is boring. Maybe it is funny. Maybe it is frightening.

That unpredictability is the same principle that makes slot machines hard to walk away from. Rewards that arrive at random keep people pulling. Researchers have compared feeds to this for years, and while the comparison is not perfect, the pull is real.
And bad news has an extra hook. Human attention is built to notice threats. A scary headline gets your eyes before a calm one does.
Now do the math. Worldwide, the average person spends about two hours and twenty one minutes a day on social media. That is the number reported for twenty twenty five.
Two hours twenty one, every day, for fifty years, adds up to about eighteen hundred days. Nearly five full years, around the clock. If you count only the hours you are awake, it is more than seven.
This is simple arithmetic on an average, not a prediction about you. But look at what it means. Seven years is about nine percent of an eighty year life.

And what does it do to focus? Professor Gloria Mark has measured how long people stay on one screen before switching. In two thousand four, it was about two and a half minutes. In studies since around twenty sixteen, she reports about forty seven seconds.
A caution. That number measures how long you stay on one screen, not how long your brain can pay attention. But it fits what most of us feel. We switch more, and we stay less.
What do studies say about doomscrolling itself? Here is what is known, and what is not.

A survey of eleven hundred American adults found about sixteen and a half percent had a severely problematic habit of consuming bad news, and heavier consumers reported more stress, anxiety and depression.
A University College London study of over a thousand people found it runs both ways. People who felt worse sought out more negative content, and the negative content made them feel worse still.

The honest caveat. Most of this is correlation, and a lot of it is self reported. Nobody has proven that scrolling alone causes depression. But the loop between feeling bad and looking at bad things is well supported.
And your feed does not only show you moods. It can pass them on. In twenty fourteen, researchers from Facebook and two universities published an experiment on emotional contagion.
When they reduced positive posts in people's feeds, those people wrote fewer positive posts and more negative ones. And the reverse was true when negative posts were reduced.
The effects were small. But across a very large number of people, it showed that emotions can spread through a screen. The study also drew criticism for running without informed consent.
Now, an honest point. Staying informed is not the problem. Caring about the world is not the problem. News can be important, and some of it is urgent.
The problem is the loop. Scrolling without a goal, with no end, with a mood that gets worse and no action that gets better.
There is a simple test. Ask, is this making me more able to do something, or just more worried? If it is only worry, you are not informing yourself. You are feeding the loop.
So how do you break it? Six steps. None of them need willpower, because willpower is the thing a feed is designed to wear down.
One. Add friction. Log out, move the app off your home screen, or delete it and use the browser. Every extra step is a chance to notice.
Two. Give it an ending. Choose news from sources that finish, a newsletter or a bulletin, instead of a feed that never does.
Three. Decide before you open it. Say out loud what you are there for, and leave when you have done it.
Four. Protect the first and last ten minutes of your day. Do not let a screen be the first or last thing you see.
Five. Replace, do not just remove. Pick the thing your thumb will do instead, a book on the table, a walk, a call.
Six. Check your weekly screen time, and set a limit you will actually keep. Small beats perfect.
One last thing. Your phone will never tell you that you have scrolled enough. It was not built to.
So you have to be the bottom of the feed. The end. The moment where you put it down.
You have probably scrolled for a while today. That is fine. The next move is the one that counts.
Put it down. Look up. That is the end of the feed.
You have reached the end.
